people.name: Galba
people.summary: Elderly aristocrat of ancient nobility, governor of Tarraconensis, who rebelled against Nero in April 68 and became the first emperor not of the Julio-Claudian house. His parsimony and severity alienated the praetorians, and he was murdered after seven months.

people.name: Piso Licinianus
people.summary: Austere young noble, descended from Crassus and Pompey, adopted by Galba on 10 January 69 and killed with him five days later.
people.death: murdered at the temple of Vesta, 15 January 69

people.name: Otho
people.summary: Nero's companion and first husband of Poppaea, exiled to govern Lusitania, who backed Galba, then murdered him and reigned for three months before killing himself after defeat at Bedriacum, a death admired even by his detractors.

people.name: Vitellius
people.summary: Son of Claudius's powerful minister Lucius Vitellius, proclaimed by the Rhine legions in January 69; his generals defeated Otho, but his reign, remembered for gluttony, collapsed before the Flavian advance and he was lynched in Rome.

people.name: Salvius Titianus
people.summary: Otho's elder brother, nominal commander of the Othonian army at the first battle of Bedriacum, pardoned by Vitellius.

people.name: Fabius Valens
people.summary: Ambitious legate who first hailed Vitellius at Cologne, led the larger Vitellian column into Italy and won Bedriacum; captured at sea while trying to raise Gaul, he was executed at Urbinum.

people.name: Caecina Alienus
people.summary: Flamboyant Vitellian general who crossed the Alps with the upper German army, won Bedriacum, then tried to defect to Vespasian before the second battle and was arrested by his men; executed by Titus in 79 for alleged conspiracy.

people.name: Vindex
people.summary: Aquitanian noble of royal descent and senator who raised Gaul against Nero in March 68 and proposed Galba as emperor; his army was destroyed by Verginius Rufus at Vesontio and he killed himself.

people.name: Verginius Rufus
people.summary: Commander who defeated Vindex but twice refused the throne offered by his legions; he lived to 83, honoured with a state funeral at which Tacitus spoke and an epitaph boasting he had claimed power for his country, not himself.

people.name: Antonius Primus
people.summary: Gallic-born adventurer, once condemned for forgery, who led the Danubian legions into Italy for Vespasian, won the second battle of Bedriacum and took Rome, only to be sidelined by Mucianus. Martial knew him in retirement at Tolosa.

people.name: Mucianus
people.summary: Governor of Syria who persuaded Vespasian to bid for power, marched the Syrian army west, and ran Rome in Vespasian's name in 70; also a writer on natural wonders quoted by Pliny.

people.name: Flavius Sabinus
people.summary: Elder brother of Vespasian and long-serving prefect of Rome, who negotiated Vitellius's abdication, was besieged on the Capitol and killed when it burned.

people.name: Vespasian
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Vespasianus Augustus (Titus Flavius Vespasianus)

roles.t: Legate of legio II Augusta in Britain

people.summary: Son of a Sabine tax-collector, a capable general in Britain and Judaea, proclaimed emperor in 69. He restored finances and order after the civil wars, rebuilt the Capitol, began the Colosseum and Temple of Peace, extended Latin rights to Spain, and founded the Flavian dynasty.
people.detail: Tacitus notes he was the only emperor changed for the better by power. Known for earthy humour (the tax on urine, 'money does not smell') and frugality. The Lex de imperio Vespasiani preserves the legal grant of his powers.

people.name: Titus
people.summary: Elder son of Vespasian, conqueror of Jerusalem (70), feared as a ruthless praetorian prefect but remembered as emperor as 'the delight of the human race' for his generosity during the Vesuvius eruption and the fire and plague of 80; he inaugurated the Colosseum and died after two years.

people.name: Domitian
people.summary: Younger son of Vespasian, an autocratic and capable administrator who raised army pay, campaigned against the Chatti, Dacians and Sarmatians, built extensively (the Palatine palace, the stadium, the Arch of Titus) and enforced morals as perpetual censor; increasingly suspicious after 89, he executed senators and was murdered by his household.
people.detail: The senatorial sources (Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius, Dio) portray a tyrant who demanded the title 'dominus et deus'; modern scholarship (Jones, Southern) credits efficient provincial administration and sound coinage. His damnatio memoriae erased his name from many inscriptions.

people.name: Domitia Longina
people.summary: Daughter of Corbulo, wife of Domitian, briefly exiled for an alleged affair with the actor Paris, and said to have known of the plot against her husband; she lived honoured into Hadrian's reign.

people.name: Berenice
people.summary: Herodian princess, sister of Agrippa II, who tried to stop Florus's massacre in 66 and became Titus's lover; she came to Rome in 75 but Titus, under popular pressure, sent her away on becoming emperor ('invitus invitam').

people.name: Tiberius Julius Alexander
people.summary: Nephew of Philo from a wealthy Alexandrian Jewish family who abandoned Judaism for an equestrian career; as prefect of Egypt he crushed Jewish riots in Alexandria (66), first proclaimed Vespasian (1 July 69), and served as Titus's second-in-command at Jerusalem.

people.name: Josephus

roles.t: Flavian client and historian in Rome

people.summary: Priestly aristocrat of Jerusalem who commanded rebel forces in Galilee, surrendered at Jotapata after predicting Vespasian's rule, served the Romans as interpreter at the siege of Jerusalem, and wrote in Rome the Jewish War, Jewish Antiquities, Life and Against Apion.
people.detail: His works are the principal source for Judaea from the Maccabees to 74 and include famous passages on John the Baptist, James and (in partly interpolated form) Jesus. Regarded by many Jews as a traitor and preserved by Christians, he remains indispensable and carefully self-justifying.

people.name: John of Gischala
people.summary: Galilean rival of Josephus who escaped to Jerusalem when Gischala fell, allied with the Zealots, and controlled the Temple during the siege of 70; he surrendered and was condemned to life imprisonment.

people.name: Simon bar Giora
people.summary: Radical rebel leader with messianic-royal pretensions who fought at Beth Horon, raised a peasant army, held the Upper City during the siege, emerged from the ruins in royal robes, and was executed at the Flavian triumph.
people.death: executed in Rome at the triumph, 71

people.name: Eleazar ben Simon
people.summary: Priestly leader of the Zealot faction, prominent in the defeat of Cestius Gallus and in control of the inner Temple until John of Gischala's men seized it at Passover 70.

people.name: Eleazar ben Yair

roles.t: Leader of the Sicarii at Masada

people.summary: Kinsman of Menahem and leader of the Sicarii at Masada, to whom Josephus attributes the speeches persuading the defenders to choose death over slavery.

people.name: Lucilius Bassus
people.summary: Admiral who brought the Ravenna fleet over to Vespasian in 69, then as legate of Judaea took Herodium and Machaerus before dying in office.

people.name: Flavius Silva
people.summary: Legate of Judaea who besieged and took Masada with legio X Fretensis; an inscription from his home town Urbs Salvia, where he built the amphitheatre, records his career.

people.name: Julius Civilis

roles.t: Batavian prince and Roman auxiliary commander

people.summary: Batavian noble of royal blood, a Roman citizen who had served 25 years in the auxilia and been twice arrested for treason, who led the Batavian revolt of 69-70; his fate after the negotiations with Cerialis is unknown. Rembrandt painted him.

people.name: Julius Classicus
people.summary: Treveran noble claiming royal descent, commander of an auxiliary cavalry unit, who proclaimed the Imperium Galliarum in 70 and made Roman legions swear allegiance to it.

people.name: Veleda
people.summary: Seeress of the Bructeri who lived in a tower on the Lippe and was consulted by intermediaries; she foretold the Batavian successes of 69, received captured Roman prisoners and a flagship, and was later captured and taken to Italy (a Greek satirical inscription from Ardea mocks her).

people.name: Munius Lupercus
people.summary: Commander of the besieged legions at Vetera, who surrendered in March 70 and was sent as a gift to the seeress Veleda but killed on the journey.

people.name: Petillius Cerialis
people.summary: Probably Vespasian's son-in-law; a dashing, reckless commander who lost legio IX's infantry to Boudica, crushed the Batavian revolt in 70 and conquered the Brigantes as governor of Britain.

people.name: Frontinus
people.summary: Governor of Britain who subdued the Silures, served in Domitian's Chattan war, and as water commissioner under Nerva wrote De aquaeductu, the key technical source on Rome's aqueducts, as well as the Strategemata.

people.name: Agricola
people.summary: Senator from Forum Iulii (Fréjus), father-in-law of Tacitus, whose seven-year governorship of Britain carried Roman arms to Mons Graupius and the Orkneys. Recalled by Domitian, he lived in quiet retirement; Tacitus's biography is his monument.
people.detail: Tacitus credits him with Romanising the British elite through baths, porticoes and banquets, 'which the ignorant called civilisation though it was part of their enslavement' (Agr. 21). The account is panegyric and much of the archaeology of his campaigns remains disputed.
people.death: illness, 23 August 93, with rumours of poison

people.name: Calgacus
people.summary: Caledonian leader at Mons Graupius, known only from Tacitus, who gives him the most famous anti-imperial speech in Latin literature ('they make a desert and call it peace').

people.name: Tacitus
people.summary: Senator, orator and the greatest Roman historian, author of the Agricola, Germania, Dialogus, Histories and Annals, whose dark, ironic analysis of the Principate from Tiberius to Domitian has dominated the modern understanding of the period.

people.name: Pliny the Elder

roles.t: Prefect of the fleet at Misenum

people.summary: Equestrian officer and polymath from Comum, friend of Vespasian, author of the 37-book Natural History and of lost histories of the German wars and of his own times; he died at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius.
people.death: asphyxiated at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius, 79

people.name: Pliny the Younger
people.summary: Nephew and adopted son of Pliny the Elder, lawyer and senator, whose nine books of literary letters, tenth book of correspondence with Trajan and Panegyricus are windows on senatorial life, the Vesuvius eruption and early Christianity.

people.name: Martial
people.summary: Epigrammatist from Bilbilis in Spain whose Book of Spectacles celebrates the Colosseum's opening and whose twelve books of epigrams depict Flavian Rome with wit and obscenity; he returned to Spain in 98.

people.name: Helvidius Priscus
people.summary: Stoic senator, son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus, exiled under Nero and executed under Vespasian for his defiant opposition; his son, also Helvidius, was executed by Domitian in 93.

people.name: Epictetus
people.summary: Phrygian-born former slave of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus, Stoic teacher expelled from Rome in 93, who taught at Nicopolis; his pupil Arrian recorded his Discourses and Handbook, admired by Marcus Aurelius.

people.name: Cornelius Fuscus
people.summary: Equestrian who declared for Vespasian in 69, Domitian's praetorian prefect, killed with much of his army invading Dacia in 86 or 87.
people.death: killed in battle in Dacia, 86 or 87

people.name: Oppius Sabinus
people.summary: Governor of Moesia killed when the Dacians crossed the frozen Danube in the winter of 85/86, opening Domitian's Dacian war.

people.name: Tettius Julianus
people.summary: Disciplinarian governor of Upper Moesia who defeated Decebalus at Tapae in 88.

people.name: Vezinas
people.summary: Dacian noble, second in rank to Decebalus, who survived the battle of Tapae in 88 by pretending to be dead and escaping at night.

people.name: Antonius Saturninus
people.summary: Governor of upper Germany proclaimed emperor at Mainz on 1 January 89; his German allies were stopped by a thaw on the Rhine and he was defeated and killed by Lappius Maximus.

people.name: Lappius Maximus
people.summary: Governor of lower Germany who crushed Saturninus's revolt in 89 and burned the rebel's papers to spare those compromised; rewarded with a second consulship (95).

people.name: Rabirius
people.summary: Domitian's architect, praised by Martial, designer of the Palatine palace (Domus Flavia and Domus Augustana), dedicated in 92.

people.name: Flavius Clemens
people.summary: Domitian's cousin, father of the emperor's designated heirs, executed for 'atheism' in 95, perhaps for Jewish or Christian sympathies; his wife Flavia Domitilla was exiled.

people.name: Decebalus
people.summary: King of Dacia who defeated Cornelius Fuscus, made a profitable peace with Domitian (89), resisted Trajan in two wars (101-102, 105-106), and killed himself rather than be captured; his head was displayed in Rome.
people.detail: Dio describes him as shrewd in strategy, knowing when to attack and when to retreat, skilled at ambushes. He used Roman engineers to fortify his Orăștie mountain capital. A 40-metre rock sculpture of his face (1994-2004) overlooks the Danube at the Iron Gates.

people.name: Nerva
people.summary: Elderly senator and jurist, a survivor who had won triumphal honours for helping suppress the Pisonian conspiracy, chosen as emperor on Domitian's murder; after a praetorian mutiny he adopted Trajan, beginning the era of the 'adoptive emperors'.

people.name: Casperius Aelianus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect under Domitian and again under Nerva, who led the guard's mutiny of 97 demanding the execution of Domitian's assassins; Trajan had him executed.

people.name: Trajan
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Nerva Traianus Augustus (Marcus Ulpius Traianus)
people.summary: First emperor born in a province, at Italica in Baetica; conqueror of Dacia (101-106) and of Armenia and Mesopotamia (114-116), annexer of Arabia, builder of the Forum, Column, Markets and Baths of Trajan, the Danube bridge and Portus's hexagonal basin, and creator of the alimenta. The Senate named him Optimus.
people.detail: Remembered as the model good emperor: later emperors were wished 'luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan', and medieval legend placed him in Paradise (Dante). His eastern conquests overreached and were abandoned by Hadrian. Sources are thin: Dio's epitome, Pliny's Panegyricus and letters, the Column.
people.death: stroke at Selinus in Cilicia, August 117

people.name: Plotina
people.summary: Wife of Trajan, admired for modesty and Epicurean learning, who championed Hadrian and announced his deathbed adoption, a story Dio suspected she staged.

people.name: Lusius Quietus
people.summary: Moorish chieftain whose cavalry fought in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian wars; he retook Nisibis and Edessa, crushed the Jews of Mesopotamia, became consul and governor of Judaea, and was executed in 118 as one of the four consulars.

people.name: Licinius Sura
people.summary: Spanish senator and Trajan's closest adviser, who helped secure his adoption and served in the Dacian wars; Trajan honoured him with a public funeral and baths on the Aventine.

people.name: Laberius Maximus
people.summary: General of the First Dacian War who captured Decebalus's sister and a strong fortress; later exiled to an island on suspicion of plotting.

people.name: Apollodorus of Damascus
people.summary: Syrian Greek architect and engineer of Trajan's Danube bridge, Forum, Markets, Baths and probably the Column; he wrote a treatise on siege engines (Poliorcetica). Dio claims Hadrian exiled and executed him for criticising his designs.

people.name: Tiberius Claudius Maximus
people.summary: Cavalry scout who brought the head of Decebalus to Trajan; his self-composed tombstone from near Philippi narrates a career from legionary cavalryman to decurion.

people.name: Pompeius Longinus
people.summary: Roman commander in Dacia treacherously captured by Decebalus in 105; he took poison so that he could not be used to extract concessions from Trajan.
people.death: suicide by poison in Dacian captivity, 105

people.name: Cornelius Palma
people.summary: Governor of Syria who annexed Nabataea as the province of Arabia in 106; executed in 118 as one of the four consulars.

people.name: Osroes I
people.summary: Arsacid king whose deposition of the Armenian king provoked Trajan's invasion; he fled from Ctesiphon in 116, losing his daughter and throne to the Romans, and later regained power.

people.name: Parthamaspates
people.summary: Son of Osroes's rival, crowned by Trajan at Ctesiphon in 116; rejected by the Parthians, he was given a lesser kingdom by Hadrian.

people.name: Marcius Turbo

roles.t: Commander against the Jewish revolt in Egypt and Cyrene

people.summary: Equestrian general who suppressed the Jewish revolts in Egypt and Cyrenaica, later governed Dacia and Pannonia together, and served Hadrian as praetorian prefect.

people.name: Attianus
people.summary: Hadrian's former guardian and Trajan's praetorian prefect, who with Plotina announced Hadrian's adoption and was blamed for the execution of the four consulars.

people.name: Hadrian
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus (Publius Aelius Hadrianus)
people.summary: Trajan's cousin and ward from Italica, who abandoned the eastern conquests, consolidated the frontiers (Hadrian's Wall, the German palisade), spent half his reign touring the provinces, codified the praetor's edict, rebuilt the Pantheon, created the Panhellenion and his villa at Tibur, and crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt.
people.detail: A passionate philhellene (the first emperor to wear a full beard), poet, amateur architect and lover of the youth Antinous, he was admired and feared; his relations with the Senate never recovered from the execution of the four consulars, and his last years were marred by illness and executions.

people.name: Sabina
people.summary: Great-niece of Trajan and wife of Hadrian in an unhappy, childless marriage; she travelled with him to Britain and Egypt (her companion Julia Balbilla carved poems on the Colossus of Memnon) and was deified after her death.

people.name: Antinous
people.summary: Bithynian youth from Claudiopolis, Hadrian's beloved, who drowned in the Nile in 130; Hadrian founded Antinoopolis and made him a god, producing one of the most widespread cults and portrait types of antiquity.

people.name: Platorius Nepos
people.summary: Friend of Hadrian and governor of Britain who began the construction of Hadrian's Wall; his name appears on building inscriptions from milecastles.

people.name: Salvius Julianus
people.fullName: Lucius Octavius Cornelius Publius Salvius Julianus Aemilianus
people.summary: North African jurist who codified the praetor's edict for Hadrian and wrote the 90-book Digesta, one of the most influential works of Roman law.

people.name: Simon bar Kokhba
people.summary: Leader of the Second Jewish Revolt, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as messiah ('son of the star'), later called Bar Koziba ('son of the lie') in rabbinic texts; his own letters survive from the Judaean desert caves.
people.death: killed at the fall of Betar, 135

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.summary: Leading sage of the generation, foundational for the Mishnah's legal method, who according to the Jerusalem Talmud hailed Bar Kosiba as messiah; tradition says he was flayed by the Romans for teaching Torah.

people.name: Tineius Rufus
people.summary: Governor of Judaea at the outbreak of the Bar Kokhba revolt, remembered in rabbinic tradition as Turnus Rufus, persecutor of Akiva.

people.name: Julius Severus
people.summary: Hadrian's best general, transferred from Britain to Judaea, who crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt by attrition and received triumphal ornaments.

people.name: Arrian
people.summary: Greek senator from Nicomedia, pupil of Epictetus (whose Discourses he recorded), governor of Cappadocia who repelled the Alans in 135, and author of the Anabasis of Alexander, the Indica, the Periplus of the Black Sea and the Order of Battle against the Alans.

people.name: Lucius Aelius Caesar
people.fullName: Lucius Aelius Caesar (born Lucius Ceionius Commodus)
people.summary: Elegant, consumptive aristocrat adopted by Hadrian as heir in 136; he died on 1 January 138, and his young son became the emperor Lucius Verus.
